content: Nocturnal enuresis, commonly known as bedwetting, is a condition that can cause significant social and emotional distress. It affects approximately 15-20% of five-year-old children and persists in up to 2% of young adults. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of complex behavioural and educational interventions for managing nocturnal enuresis in children and to compare these interventions with other treatment options. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. They included all randomised or quasi-randomised trials that investigated complex behavioural or educational interventions for nocturnal enuresis in children. However, studies focusing solely on daytime wetting were excluded. The comparison groups included no treatment, simple behavioural methods, physical interventions, bedwetting alarms, desmopressin, tricyclic antidepressants, and other miscellaneous treatments. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the eligible trials and extracted the data. A total of 18 trials involving 1,174 children were identified. These trials examined the use of complex or educational interventions for nocturnal enuresis. However, many of the studies were small in scale and had methodological limitations, such as quasi-randomised allocation methods in three trials and baseline differences between groups in another three trials. The findings indicated that complex interventions, such as dry bed training (DBT) or full spectrum home training (FSHT), when combined with a bedwetting alarm, were more effective than no treatment. For example, the relative risk (RR) of failure or relapse after stopping DBT was 0.25 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.39) compared to no treatment. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of complex interventions when used without an alarm. When comparing interventions, a bedwetting alarm alone was found to be more effective than DBT alone. For instance, the RR of failure or relapse after DBT alone versus DBT combined with an alarm was 2.81 (95% CI 1.80 to 4.38). On the other hand, combining a complex intervention with a bedwetting alarm appeared to reduce the relapse rate compared to using an alarm alone. For example, the RR of failure or relapse after DBT plus an alarm versus an alarm alone was 0.5 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.80). There was insufficient evidence to determine whether providing educational information about enuresis, regardless of the method of delivery, was effective. However, there was some evidence suggesting that direct contact between families and therapists enhanced the effectiveness of complex interventions. Additionally, increased contact and support appeared to improve the outcomes of simple behavioural interventions, although these findings were based on single trials and require confirmation through further randomised controlled trials. Future research should also evaluate the impact of these interventions on resource use. In conclusion, while DBT and FSHT were more effective than no treatment when combined with a bedwetting alarm, there is not enough evidence to support their use without an alarm. A bedwetting alarm alone was more effective than DBT alone, but combining an alarm with DBT appeared to provide additional benefits. There is also preliminary evidence that direct therapist involvement may enhance the effectiveness of interventions, but further research is needed to confirm these findings.
